lessons.title: Read logarithms as powers
lessons.summary: Convert between powers and logarithms. Use positive arguments, including fractional and negative powers.
lessons.objective: Convert between powers and logarithms. Use positive arguments, including fractional and negative powers.
lessons.before: Read a log statement as a question about an exponent. For a legal base, each positive argument has one corresponding power.
lessons.ideas:
The statements \(b^u=v\) and \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) have the same meaning when \(b>0,\ b\ne1,\ v>0\).

For unknown positive \(b\), \(\log_{b}\left(v\right)=u\) gives \(b=v^{1/u}\) if \(u\ne0\) and the answer is a legal base.

For a logarithm of a whole expression, require that whole expression to be greater than zero, for example \(\lg(5x-1)\) needs \(x>\tfrac15\).
lessons.method:
Try to rewrite the base and argument as powers of one smaller base.

Check the recovered base is positive and different from one.

Solve the argument inequality before solving the log equation.
mistakes: The logarithm is the exponent. Keep the base and the argument in their own roles.
Multiplying by a fractional exponent is different from raising to that exponent.
The boundary itself is excluded because the argument is zero there.

examples.title: Read a logarithm as a power
examples.question:
A scale uses the base \(16\).

  1. Give the exact value of \(\log_{16}\left(64\right)\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact increase in the logarithm when the argument changes to \(256\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Write the base and argument as powers of \(4\).

If the logarithm is \(x\), then \(4^{(2)x}=4^{3}\). Match exponents.

\(\frac{3}{2}\)

(b) The new exponent in base \(4\) is \(4\).

The change in base \(16\) is \(2-\frac{3}{2}\).

\(\frac{1}{2}\)

examples.title: Find an unknown logarithm base
examples.question:
The base \(b\) is a positive real number other than 1. The reading is \(\log_{b}\left(81\right)=2\).

  1. Find \(b\).

    [2]

  2. Hence find \(\log_{b}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Translate the logarithm to \(b^{2}=81\).

Raise each side to the reciprocal power \(\frac{1}{2}\). The right side is the square of \(3\).

\(9\)

(b) The argument is \(3^{-1}\), while the base is \(3^{2}\).

To make the power \(-1\), multiply \(2\) by \(-\tfrac12\).

\(-\tfrac12\)

examples.title: Unwrap a logarithmic expression
examples.question:
Let \(g(x)=\log_{6}\left(2x+3\right)\) on its natural domain.

  1. State the domain of \(g\), in interval notation or as an inequality.

    [2]

  2. Find the unique solution of \(g(x)=2\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The argument must be strictly positive: \(2x+3>0\).

The coefficient of \(x\) is positive. Divide without reversing the inequality.

\(x>-\frac{3}{2}\)

(b) Use the definition of the logarithm, so that \(2x+3=6^{2}\).

Subtract \(3\) and divide by \(2\).

\(x=\frac{33}{2}\)

lessons.title: Laws of logarithms
lessons.summary: Use the product, quotient and power laws to combine and evaluate logarithms.
lessons.objective: Use the product, quotient and power laws to combine and evaluate logarithms.
lessons.before: Dividing powers of the same number subtracts their exponents. Logarithms return those exponents.
lessons.ideas:
With positive arguments \(A,B\), \(\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=\log_{b}\left(\tfrac{A}{B}\right)\).

Use \(n\log_{b}\left(x\right)=\log_{b}\left(x^n\right)\) before applying the product and quotient laws. Each original argument must be positive.

If \(A=b^u\) and \(B=b^v\), then \(k\log_{b}\left(A\right)-\log_{b}\left(B\right)=ku-v\).
lessons.method:
Keep the order of arguments: the subtracted log supplies the denominator.

For symbolic arguments, write the combined argument clearly before simplifying it.

Check your evaluation by combining the logs and simplifying the powers inside.
mistakes: Subtracting the arguments gives a different number. Form the quotient first.
No log law replaces a logarithm of a sum by a sum of logarithms.
The coefficient multiplies the value of its own logarithm. It does not multiply the log base.

examples.title: Use the quotient law before evaluating
examples.question:
Consider \(L=\log_{3}\left(648\right)-\log_{3}\left(8\right)\).

  1. Evaluate L exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the value of \(\log_{3}\left(8\right)+L\) as a single logarithm to base \(3\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The difference of logs has argument \(\frac{648}{8}=81\).

Since \(3^{4}=81\), the logarithm is \(4\).

\(4\)

(b) Rewrite \(L\) as \(\log_{3}\left(81\right)\).

Adding logarithms with the same base multiplies their arguments.

\(\log_{3}\left(648\right)\)

examples.title: Combine three logarithms into one
examples.question:
For \(x>0\), consider \(2\log_{4}\left(x\right)+\log_{4}\left(3\right)-\log_{4}\left(3\right)\).

  1. Write this expression as a single logarithm to base \(4\).

    [2]

  2. Solve the equation obtained by setting the original expression equal to \(\log_{4}\left(4\right)\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Move \(2\) into the exponent of \(x\), giving \(\log_{4}\left(x^2\right)\).

Multiply the first two arguments and divide by \(3\).

\(\log_{4}\left(x^2\right)\)

(b) Logarithms with the same legal base are one-to-one.

Equate the arguments, cancel their common coefficient and solve \(x^2=4\). Keep the positive value.

\(x=2\)

examples.title: Use a power before subtracting logarithms
examples.question:
The value \(D\) is defined by \(D=3\log_{2}\left(4\right)-\log_{2}\left(16\right)\).

  1. Evaluate D exactly.

    [2]

  2. Write \(2^{D}\) as a rational number.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The individual logarithms are \(2\) and \(4\).

Substitute into the expression to get \(3\times2-4=2\).

\(2\)

(b) Substitute the value of \(D\) into the exponent.

A negative exponent means a reciprocal.

\(4\)

lessons.title: Change the base of a logarithm
lessons.summary: Use a common base, work with given log values and interpret reciprocals.
lessons.objective: Use a common base, work with given log values and interpret reciprocals.
lessons.before: Turn the log into an exponential equation, take logs in a new base, then solve for the original exponent. A base shared by both numbers can give an exact rational result.
lessons.ideas:
For any legal new base \(c\), \(\log_{a}\left(b\right)=\frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}\).

The numerator of \(\log_{b}\left(a^n\right)\) after changing to base 10 is \(\lg(a^n)=n\lg a\).

When \(a,b>0\) and both differ from 1, \(\frac{1}{\log_{a}\left(b\right)}=\log_{b}\left(a\right)\).
lessons.method:
Choose a common small base if both numbers are powers of it.

Keep the ratio exact until the required answer is obtained.

Check that the original logarithm is nonzero before taking its reciprocal.
mistakes: Apply the same new base to numerator and denominator. The original base is in the denominator.
Include the power as a multiplier after changing the base.
A reciprocal is a fraction with numerator 1. It is different from an inverse function.

examples.title: Choose a shared base to compare two logarithms
examples.question:
The two numbers used in a scaling rule are \(A=46656\) and \(B=7776\).

  1. Find \(\log_{A}\left(B\right)\) exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\log_{B}\left(A\right)+\log_{A}\left(B\right)\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Changing to base \(6\) gives \(\frac{\log_{6}\left(B\right)}{\log_{6}\left(A\right)}\).

The numerator is \(5\) and the denominator is \(6\).

\(\frac{5}{6}\)

(b) Reversing the base and argument inverts the ratio of the two logarithms.

Add \(\frac{5}{6}\) to \(\frac{6}{5}\).

\(\frac{61}{30}\)

examples.title: Use known logarithms as data
examples.question:
Positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy \(\lg a=10,\quad \lg b=2\).

  1. Find \(\log_{b}\left(a^6\right)\) without evaluating \(a\) or \(b\).

    [2]

  2. Evaluate \(\log_{a}\left(b^6\right)\) exactly.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Change to base 10. The numerator becomes \(6\lg a\) using the power law.

Divide \(60\) by \(2\).

\(30\)

(b) Change to base 10 again, but now the numerator is \(6\lg b\).

The denominator is \(\lg a\).

\(\frac{6}{5}\)

examples.title: Simplify a reciprocal of a logarithm
examples.question:
Here a reciprocal means the number 1 divided by the logarithm. Let \(R=\frac{1}{\log_{4}\left(8\right)}\).

  1. Find R exactly.

    [2]

  2. Verify that \(\log_{8}\left(4\right)\) equals R using a common base.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The inner log is \(\frac{3}{2}\) because \(4\) and \(8\) are powers of \(2\).

Invert this value, or interchange the base and the argument using change of base.

\(\frac{2}{3}\)

(b) Write the new base as \(2^{3}\) and the argument as \(2^{2}\).

The exponent must be \(\frac{2}{3}\).

\(\log_{8}\left(4\right)=\frac{2}{3}\)

lessons.title: Solve logarithmic equations
lessons.summary: Check domains first, solve a combined equation and test every candidate in the original logarithms.
lessons.objective: Check domains first, solve a combined equation and test every candidate in the original logarithms.
lessons.before: State the restriction first. Convert the log equality into exponential form. Then solve the simpler algebraic equation and check the original argument.
lessons.ideas:
Use \(\log_{a}\left(U\right)=r\) to obtain \(U=a^r\). The function requires \(U>0\).

A solution must make each original argument positive. The condition \(UV>0\) alone is weaker than \(U>0\) and \(V>0\) together.

Set the quotient of the original arguments to \(a^r\) when their log difference in base \(a\) equals \(r\). Check that the denominator is positive.
lessons.method:
Show the original domain even when you expect only one candidate.

Write a rejection reason beside any candidate you exclude.

At the end, substitute to confirm that both log arguments are positive.
mistakes: The right-hand side of the new equation is a power of the log base.
Do not accept a quadratic root without testing the original arguments.
Cross-multiplying before noting the domain can introduce candidates excluded by an original argument.

examples.title: Solve an equation with one logarithm
examples.question:
Consider \(\log_{7}\left(7x-3\right)=3\).

  1. Find the exact solution.

    [2]

  2. State the domain of the logarithm in the original equation.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Rewrite the equation as \(7x-3=343\).

Add \(3\) and divide by \(7\). The argument is \(343\), so it is positive.

\(x=\frac{346}{7}\)

(b) Set \(7x-3>0\). Divide by the positive coefficient.

\(x>\frac{3}{7}\)

examples.title: Solve a product of positive log arguments
examples.question:
Solve \(\log_{5}\left(x-12\right)+\log_{5}\left(x+612\right)=4\) over the reals.

  1. Give the valid solution.

    [3]

  2. Show why the rejected quadratic root cannot solve the original equation.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Both arguments must be positive. The stronger restriction is \(x>12\).

Combine the logs and solve \((x-12)(x+612)=625\).

The candidates are \(13\) and \(-613\). Only \(13\) satisfies the restriction.

\(x=13\)

(b) At \(x=-613\), the first argument equals \(-625\). A real logarithm of that value does not exist.

Its first argument is negative.

examples.title: Solve a quotient equation and keep the domain
examples.question:
Consider \(\log_{3}\left(12x-15\right)-\log_{3}\left(x-1\right)=2\).

  1. Find the exact value of x.

    [2]

  2. Evaluate the first logarithm at the solution.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The original arguments require \(x>\frac{5}{4}\) and \(x>1\).

Combine to a quotient and rearrange to \(12x-15=9(x-1)\).

Collect like terms. At \(2\), the arguments are \(9\) and \(1\), so the value is valid.

\(2\)

(b) The first argument evaluates to \(9\).

This is \(3^{2}\).

\(2\)

lessons.title: Solve exponential equations
lessons.summary: Use a common base, logarithms or a positive substitution depending on the equation.
lessons.objective: Use a common base, logarithms or a positive substitution depending on the equation.
lessons.before: Look for a small common base before taking any logarithms. Since legal exponential functions pass each positive value once, equal outputs give equal exponents.
lessons.ideas:
If \(b>0\) and \(b\ne1\), then \(b^u=b^v\) implies \(u=v\).

For \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\) and \(b>0\), the solution of \(a^x=b\) is \(x=\frac{\ln b}{\ln a}\).

With \(u=a^x\), the expression \(a^{2x}\) becomes \(u^2\) and \(u>0\).
lessons.method:
State the common base in your working, then solve a linear equation if possible.

Keep the exact ratio during working and round only if the question asks for it.

For each positive solution in u, solve a separate exponential equation for x.
mistakes: When changing the base of a power, multiply the entire exponent by the extra power.
If a constant has been added outside the exponential, move it before taking logs.
A negative or zero value of the substituted variable cannot be an exponential value.

examples.title: Solve by rewriting two powers in one base
examples.question:
The equation is \(256^{2x+1}=256^{6}\).

  1. Find x exactly.

    [2]

  2. Hence solve \(256^{2x+1}=256^{7}\) exactly.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Write the two bases as powers of \(4\).

Equate the exponents to get \(4(2x+1)=24\). Solve for \(x\).

\(\frac{5}{2}\)

(b) The exponent on the right increases by \(4\) in base \(4\).

The exponent on the left grows by \(8\) per unit of \(x\).

\(3\)

examples.title: Solve an exponential equation with logarithms
examples.question:
Consider the equation \(6^{3x+1}=27\).

  1. Give the value of x correct to 3 decimal places.

    [3]

  2. If the right-hand side is multiplied by \(6\), by how much does the solution increase? Give an exact value.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Take natural logarithms of both sides, giving \((3x+1)\ln 6=\ln 27\).

Collect the terms to get \(x=\frac{\ln 27-1\ln 6}{3\ln 6}\). Round at the end.

\(x\approx 0.280\)

(b) Multiplying the output by the base \(6\) increases the exponent by 1.

Since the exponent has gradient \(3\), x increases by \(\frac{1}{3}\).

\(\frac{1}{3}\)

examples.title: Reduce two exponential terms to a quadratic
examples.question:
Consider \(3^{2x+6}-36\cdot 3^{x+3}+243=0\).

  1. Find both exact x-values.

    [3]

  2. Explain what happens if one root of the substituted quadratic is negative.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Set \(u=3^{x+3}\). The first term becomes \(u^2\).

The quadratic factors as \((u-9)(u-27)=0\).

Both u-values are positive. Match the exponent \(x+3\) to \(2\) and \(3\) in turn.

\(x=-1\text{ or }x=0\)

(b) For real x, the value of \(3^{x+3}\) is positive.

It cannot give a real solution for x.

lessons.title: Natural logarithms and substitutions
lessons.summary: Simplify inverse operations to base e and find intersections by replacing ln x with a new variable.
lessons.objective: Simplify inverse operations to base e and find intersections by replacing ln x with a new variable.
lessons.before: The natural logarithm is the logarithm to base e. It takes a positive value back to its exponent.
lessons.ideas:
For real \(t\), \(\ln(e^t)=t\). For \(x>0\), \(e^{\ln x}=x\).

When \(A>0\), \(\ln(Ae^u)=\ln A+u\).

Take \(t=\ln x\), solve for t, then recover \(x=e^t\). The variable t can take any real value.
lessons.method:
Cancel inverse operations symbolically instead of approximating e.

Use the product law before finding the final numerical value.

Find the matching y-value for each recovered x-coordinate.
mistakes: The second identity only works when the original log argument is positive.
A constant inside a product becomes a logarithmic term, not the constant itself.
The substituted t-values are not the x-coordinates.

examples.title: Undo a natural exponential without approximating e
examples.question:
A reading satisfies \(e^{11x+3}=e^{5}\).

  1. Find x exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(\ln\left(e^{x}\right)+1\) at this reading.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The natural logarithm reverses an exponential to base e.

Taking natural logs gives \(11x+3=5\). Rearrange to isolate x.

\(\frac{2}{11}\)

(b) The natural log cancels the exponential, leaving \(x+1\).

Substitute \(\frac{2}{11}\).

\(\frac{13}{11}\)

examples.title: Cancel a product inside a natural logarithm
examples.question:
For real x, define \(F(x)=\ln\left(10e^{3x}\right)-\ln\left(10\right)\).

  1. Find the exact solution to \(F(x)=7\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact value of \(F(-1)\).

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) By the quotient law, the logarithm argument simplifies to \(e^{3x}\).

The left-hand side becomes \(3x\).

\(\frac{7}{3}\)

(b) Use the simplified form \(F(x)=3x\).

\(-3\)

examples.title: Find intersections using a log substitution
examples.question:
For \(x>0\), the two curves are \(y=6\ln x\) and \(y=(\ln x)^2-6\ln x+35\).

  1. At the intersections, find both values of ln x.

    [2]

  2. State the exact coordinates of both intersections.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Set \(t=\ln x\) and equate the two y-expressions.

After subtraction the equation is \((t-5)(t-7)=0\).

\(\ln x=5\text{ or }\ln x=7\)

(b) Exponentiate both t-values to get the original x-values.

Compute y from \(y=6\ln x\) at each solution.

\((e^{5},30)\text{ and }(e^{7},42)\)

lessons.title: Exponential growth and decay models
lessons.summary: Use a multiplicative model to recover constants, predict readings and solve threshold questions.
lessons.objective: Use a multiplicative model to recover constants, predict readings and solve threshold questions.
lessons.before: In a multiplicative model the same positive factor applies over equal time intervals. Divide the later observation by the earlier one to cancel the scale.
lessons.ideas:
For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the ratio over \(\Delta t\) time units is \(b^{\Delta t}\). The positive root recovers b.

For positive \(A,k,L\), \(Ae^{-kt}=L\) gives \(t=\frac{\ln(A/L)}{k}\) and represents non-negative time when \(L\le A\).

For \(P(t)=Ab^t\), the reference reading is \(P(0)=A\) and the reading one interval earlier is \(P(-1)=\frac{A}{b}\).
lessons.method:
Record the elapsed time between observations, not the final time label.

Interpret the final value in the units given for time.

Distinguish the reference time from the first time the process really existed.
mistakes: The ratio of observations may describe several intervals. It is not automatically the one-step factor.
The minus sign belongs to the rate in the exponent. Check that a decay time is non-negative.
A model prediction outside the measured interval is an extrapolation.

examples.title: Recover the scale and growth multiplier
examples.question:
A controlled simulation reports \(G=Ab^t\) with positive constants. The readings are \(G(1)=24\) and \(G(5)=\frac{497664}{625}\).

TimeReading
\(1\)\(24\)
\(5\)\(\frac{497664}{625}\)

  1. Find the growth multiplier \(b\) exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find \(A\) and then the exact next reading \(G(6)\).

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Divide the second reading by the first. There are \(4\) time steps between them.

The ratio is \(\frac{20736}{625}\), so take its positive \(4\)th root.

\(\frac{12}{5}\)

(b) Divide the first reading by b to find A.

The next value is the most recent reading multiplied by \(\frac{12}{5}\).

\(A=10\text{ and }G(6)=\frac{5971968}{3125}\)

examples.title: Find when an exponential decay model reaches a threshold
examples.question:
A sensor records \(R=21e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}\) for time t in hours. The alert level is \(\frac{21}{4}\).

  1. Find the time at which the reading reaches the alert level. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [2]

  2. Explain why this is the only non-negative time when the alert level is met.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Divide by \(21\). This gives \(e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Take logs and divide by the negative coefficient of t, obtaining \(t=\frac{-\ln(\frac{1}{4})}{\frac{1}{5}}\).

\(6.931\text{ h}\)

(b) The exponent has a strictly negative coefficient and the positive scale is \(21\). The reading starts above the threshold and tends to 0.

The exponential factor is strictly decreasing, so it passes through that level once.

examples.title: Interpret a measured multiplicative change
examples.question:
A reading obeys \(R(t)=A\,b^t\). At the reference time \(t=0\), it is \(20\). Over the next \(6\) intervals it becomes \(20\).

  1. Find the exact value of \(b\).

    [2]

  2. Find the value predicted one interval before the reference time. Explain the interpretation of this calculation.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The reference reading gives \(A=20\).

Divide the later reading by the reference reading and take the positive \(6\)th root.

\(1\)

(b) Divide rather than multiply to move back one time interval.

This is a backward extrapolation of the model. Its accuracy depends on whether that model was valid before the reference time.

\(R(-1)=20\)

lessons.title: Graphs of shifted exponentials
lessons.summary: Find intercepts, asymptotes, range and direction for y = k eⁿˣ + a.
lessons.objective: Find intercepts, asymptotes, range and direction for y = k eⁿˣ + a.
lessons.before: Follow the direction in which the exponential term tends to zero. That is where the graph approaches its asymptote.
lessons.ideas:
For \(y=ke^{nx}+a\) with \(kn\ne0\), the asymptote is \(y=a\). The y-intercept is \((0,k+a)\).

For \(y=ke^{nx}+a\), a crossing requires \(-a/k>0\). Taking logs then gives its exact x-coordinate.

At \(x=0\), the exponential is \(e^0=1\). The intercept is the sum of the scale and the shift.
lessons.method:
Mark the asymptote with a dashed line and draw the curve on the correct side.

Check the side of the asymptote before searching for a crossing.

Keep inferred parameters separate from supplied graph features.
mistakes: The graph generally crosses the vertical axis at a different height from its horizontal asymptote.
The exponent at a crossing need not be zero. First move the vertical translation.
The intercept and asymptote alone give no information about the rate in the exponent.

examples.title: Read the asymptote and intercepts of an exponential graph
examples.question:
The curve has equation \(y=-4e^{x}+5\).

  1. State the equation of its horizontal asymptote.

    [2]

  2. State the y-intercept and range, and sketch the graph.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) The exponential term tends to zero as x tends to negative infinity.

The remaining vertical shift is \(5\).

\(y=5\)

(b) At x = 0, the exponential term is one.

The curve lies below its asymptote because the exponential factor stays positive.

The sign of the coefficient product \(-4\) gives the direction of movement as x increases.

\((0,1)\) and \(y<5\). The graph is decreasing.

examples.title: Locate an exponential graph's x-axis intercept
examples.question:
Consider \(y=7e^{4x}-11\).

  1. Find the x-coordinate of the intercept. Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

    [2]

  2. For a line \(y=c\), state the condition on c for one intersection with this curve.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) On the x-axis, y is zero. Isolate the exponential to get \(e^{4x}=\frac{11}{7}\).

The exact coordinate is \(\frac{\ln(\frac{11}{7})}{4}\). Round only at the end.

\(x\approx 0.113\)

(b) The exponential term is always positive, and can take every positive value. The entire range lies above \(-11\).

\(c>-11\)

examples.title: Recover parameters of a shifted exponential
examples.question:
The graph of \(y=ke^{2x}+a\) passes through \((0,13)\). Its horizontal asymptote is \(y=10\).

  1. Find the value of k.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact height of the graph when \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The asymptote gives \(a=10\).

At the y-intercept the exponential is 1. Subtract \(10\) from the intercept.

\(3\)

(b) At this x, the exponent is 1. Multiply e by \(3\) and add \(10\).

\(3e+10\)

lessons.title: Graphs of transformed logarithms
lessons.summary: Use argument positivity, the boundary and both intercepts to sketch y = k ln(ax + b).
lessons.objective: Use argument positivity, the boundary and both intercepts to sketch y = k ln(ax + b).
lessons.before: First find the input where the argument would be zero. The graph is on the side where the argument is positive, even if that is to the left.
lessons.ideas:
For \(y=k\ln(ax+b)\), find the domain from \(ax+b>0\). The equality gives the vertical asymptote.

At the x-intercept solve \(ax+b=1\). For a y-intercept, check \(x=0\) lies in the domain, then evaluate.

The sign of \(ka\) gives the direction of \(y=k\ln(ax+b)\) on its domain. A positive sign gives an increasing curve.
lessons.method:
State the asymptote as an equation of a vertical line.

Label both the crossing and the asymptote if they are visible.

A sketch requires the valid side of the asymptote as well as the direction of the graph.
mistakes: With a negative inner coefficient the domain inequality reverses when you divide.
Setting the argument equal to zero gives the asymptote only.
Check both signs. Reflecting inputs and reflecting outputs have different geometric effects.

examples.title: Locate the boundary and intercept of a logarithmic curve
examples.question:
A curve has equation \(y=3\ln\left(-6x+12\right)\).

  1. State the natural domain.

    [2]

  2. Find the x-intercept and the equation of the vertical asymptote. Sketch the curve.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Solve \(-6x+12>0\). Dividing by the negative coefficient reverses the inequality.

\(x<2\)

(b) A logarithm is zero when its argument reaches 1. Solve \(-6x+12=1\).

The domain boundary occurs at argument 0. The graph never reaches that vertical line.

examples.title: Recover the log argument from its vertical asymptote

    [2]

  2. Find the exact x-intercept and y-intercept.

    [3]

(a) At the asymptote the argument tends to 0. Set \(3(-8)+b=0\).

\(24\)

(b) Solve \(3x+24=1\) at the x-intercept.

  1. State the natural domain.

    [3]
examples.solution:
(a) Solve \(-2x+9>0\). Dividing by the negative coefficient reverses the inequality.

\(x<\frac{9}{2}\)

(b) A logarithm is zero when its argument reaches 1. Solve \(-2x+9=1\).

lessons.title: Inverse logarithmic and exponential functions
lessons.summary: Find inverse rules and exchange domain with range.
lessons.objective: Find inverse rules and exchange domain with range.
lessons.before: Name the output y, remove any translation and scale, take the logarithm and divide by the coefficient of x. Then use x as the inverse input.
lessons.ideas:
Inverting \(y=ke^{nx}+a\) uses \(x=\frac1n\ln\left(\frac{y-a}{k}\right)\). The quotient inside ln must be positive.

If \(y=k\ln(ax+b)\), then \(ax+b=e^{y/k}\). Preserve the original input restriction when giving the inverse range.

To find \(f^{-1}(c)\), solve \(f(x)=c\). Where f is one-to-one, the equation has at most one solution.
lessons.method:
Recover the inverse domain from the original range.

Check the inverse outputs stay on the valid side of the original asymptote.

Use the original definition to check any numerical inverse value.
mistakes: Subtract the shift and divide by the scale before applying the logarithm.
Dividing by the multiplier outside the log is different from dividing its argument.
The notation for an inverse function does not mean a reciprocal.

examples.title: Invert a translated exponential
examples.question:
The function \(f(x)=2e^{7x}+7\) is defined for all real x.

  1. Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).

    [2]

  2. State the domain of the inverse and explain why it has this domain.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Let y be the original output. Isolate the exponential as \(e^{7x}=\frac{y-7}{2}\).

Take natural logs and divide by \(7\). Write the original output as the variable of the inverse.

\(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{7}\ln\left(\frac{x-7}{2}\right)\)

(b) The original outputs are strictly above \(7\). These become the allowed inputs of the inverse.

The positivity condition on the argument of the inverse logarithm gives the same result.

\(x>7\)

examples.title: Invert a logarithmic rule
examples.question:
Let \(h(x)=5\ln\left(5x-5\right)\) on its natural domain.

  1. Find \(h^{-1}(x)\).

    [2]

  2. State the exact range and domain of the inverse.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Divide the original equation by \(5\), then exponentiate to obtain the original argument.

Add \(5\) and divide by \(5\) to isolate the original input.

\(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^{\frac{1}{5}x}+5}{5}\)

(b) The original allowed inputs are \(x>1\). Those become inverse outputs.

A natural logarithm covers every real output. All real x therefore work in the inverse.

\(y>1\). The inverse is defined for every real x.

examples.title: Evaluate an inverse via the original rule
examples.question:
The function is \(f(x)=\log_{8}\left(8x-9\right)\) on its natural domain.

  1. Find the exact value of \(f^{-1}(1)\).

    [2]

  2. State the value of \(f(f^{-1}(1))\) and explain the result.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) If \(x\) is the inverse value, the original output at x must be \(1\).

Solve \(8x-9=8\).

\(\frac{17}{8}\)

(b) The inverse starts from the target output and recovers the input that produced it. Applying the original function returns that output.

\(1\)

questions.prompt_html:

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Both arguments must be positive. The stronger restriction is \(x>13\).

Combine the logs and solve \((x-13)(x-7)=7\).

The candidates are \(14\) and \(6\). Only \(14\) satisfies the restriction.

\(x=14\)

questions.prompt_html:

This is \(5^{1}\).

\(1\)

questions.title: Solve an exponential equation with logarithms
questions.prompt_html:
Consider the equation \(6^{3x+3}=30\).

  1. Give the value of x correct to 3 decimal places.

    [3]

  2. If the right-hand side is multiplied by \(6\), by how much does the solution increase? Give an exact value.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Take natural logarithms of both sides, giving \((3x+3)\ln 6=\ln 30\).

Collect the terms to get \(x=\frac{\ln 30-3\ln 6}{3\ln 6}\). Round at the end.

\(x\approx -0.367\)

(b) Multiplying the output by the base \(6\) increases the exponent by 1.

Since the exponent has gradient \(3\), x increases by \(\frac{1}{3}\).

\(\frac{1}{3}\)

  1. Find both exact x-values.

    [3]

questions.answer_html:
(a) \(x=-1\text{ or }x=1\)

questions.solution_html:
(a) Set \(u=2^{x+3}\). The first term becomes \(u^2\).

The quadratic factors as \((u-4)(u-16)=0\).

Both u-values are positive. Match the exponent \(x+3\) to \(2\) and \(4\) in turn.

\(x=-1\text{ or }x=1\)

(b) For real x, the value of \(2^{x+3}\) is positive.

It cannot give a real solution for x.

The function \(f(x)=7e^{5x}+5\) is defined for all real x.

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
questions.solution_html:
Let y be the original output. Isolate the exponential as \(e^{5x}=\frac{y-5}{7}\).

Take natural logs and divide by \(5\). Write the original output as the variable of the inverse.

\(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{5}\ln\left(\frac{x-5}{7}\right)\)
questions.hint_html: Isolate the original exponential before taking logs.

questions.title: Invert a logarithmic rule
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(h(x)=2\ln\left(5x-5\right)\) on its natural domain.

Find \(h^{-1}(x)\).
questions.solution_html:
Divide the original equation by \(2\), then exponentiate to obtain the original argument.

Add \(5\) and divide by \(5\) to isolate the original input.

\(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^{\frac{1}{2}x}+5}{5}\)
questions.hint_html: Divide by the outside multiplier first, then undo ln with e to a power.

questions.title: Evaluate an inverse via the original rule
questions.prompt_html:
The function is \(f(x)=\log_{6}\left(5x-3\right)\) on its natural domain.

questions.solution_html:

Solve \(5x-3=216\).

questions.title: Invert a translated exponential
questions.prompt_html:
The function \(f(x)=3e^{2x}+13\) is defined for all real x.

  1. Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).

    [2]

  2. State the domain of the inverse and explain why it has this domain.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Let y be the original output. Isolate the exponential as \(e^{2x}=\frac{y-13}{3}\).

Take natural logs and divide by \(2\). Write the original output as the variable of the inverse.

\(f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{x-13}{3}\right)\)

(b) The original outputs are strictly above \(13\). These become the allowed inputs of the inverse.

The positivity condition on the argument of the inverse logarithm gives the same result.

\(x>13\)

questions.title: Invert a logarithmic rule
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(h(x)=6\ln\left(5x-2\right)\) on its natural domain.

  1. Find \(h^{-1}(x)\).

    [2]

  2. State the exact range and domain of the inverse.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^{\frac{1}{6}x}+2}{5}\)

(b) \(y>\frac{2}{5}\). The inverse is defined for every real x.
questions.solution_html:
(a) Divide the original equation by \(6\), then exponentiate to obtain the original argument.

Add \(2\) and divide by \(5\) to isolate the original input.

\(h^{-1}(x)=\frac{e^{\frac{1}{6}x}+2}{5}\)

(b) The original allowed inputs are \(x>\frac{2}{5}\). Those become inverse outputs.

A natural logarithm covers every real output. All real x therefore work in the inverse.

\(y>\frac{2}{5}\). The inverse is defined for every real x.
